I thought I would start a new thread on this topic.

> **JohnFP:** Seventh Son, you mention you want your gelatin hard before humidifying it. How is "Hard" being used here. Are you saying hard in meaning moisture contect and thus you store you film in low relative humidity to dry (either low ambient humidity or controlled low humidity for humid areas). I imagine that would be around 30 - 35% relative humidy due to your statement do humidify at 45 - 60%. Is this correct?Also, in which way do you change your formula for winter and summer. If summer is more humid then do you lower water amount when making emulsion? And how does this make the film "Harder". Or do you add water in summer to get a thinner coating which can dry a little harder?How do you coat?Thanks in advace,John

> **Seventh Son:** Greetings John FP,There are so many possible variables it's hard to know where to begin.Maybe I shouldn’t have used the word hard. I think perhaps dense would be a better descriptor. I use a formula that is very dense, in that it doesn’t readily accept the requisite chemical development. Why do I do this? Color control, Clarity control, and Brightness control. If I use a film that is ready to go 24hrs after coating it is more sensitive to ambient RH. I want my film to behave in very specific ways, so I control the amount of pre-exposure RH to get expected results.Try it on smaller pieces of film, and see if you like the results.Yes, I add water during the driest part of the year. Or, I can also increase my RH.I spin coat.I hope any part of this is helpful.

I think I understand now and will be implementing this technique shortly. 

But I must say, I may have to modify or adapt it as I truly want to start making plain gelatin plates that can keep forever in the fridge and then sensitize when needed. Any adivise on Humidification using this technique? 

My best guess is as follows and right now it is only a educated guess. Any Comments?

Make the gelatin solution as I do emulsion, same cooking parameters.

Filter.

Veil and spin coat.

Place plate in a dry area, maybe even sunlight after a couple of hours to completely dry and densify it. 

Store it in fridge.

Prior to using it, allow the gelatin to be exposed to a slow and steady RH as you describe which is what the entire lab is in my third world basement (about 68F and 60 - 65 RH).

Then dip the plate in an AmDi solution of desired concentration.

Blot off excess and clean back.

Allow exposure to the same Ambient Temp and RH for the desired time.

Shoot.

Now do you think all control prior to sensitizing really does not matter much because there is no AmDi in the emulsion to actually dark react crosslink? And it may be as long as I get the gelatin nice and dry/dense/hard, then I can simply put it in the sensitizer then allow it to stablize at my 68F and 60RH for the desired time?

The beauty with this technique is not only a grealy reduces prep time to make a hologram but since the gelatin has no sensitizer in it, I could acually fabricate it anywhere the humidity is low.

posts.author: Ed Wesly
posts.content_md:
As always, it's a matter of getting something to work for yourself. When I did DCG yers ago, I was never successful with mixing the dichromate with the gel; it always crystallized out. Something was not working right, my gel, (Knox), my dichromate, my glass, my recipe, my body odor, whatever.

Then I switched to the approach that 7th Son mentions, pre-coating the glass and sensitizing later. At the end of the first day, I would coat the plates with gel and a Mayer bar, and "dry" them under a HEPA hood with trays of water next to the plates, so they were dried under high humidity conditions. I got this tip from none other than the DCG'er extraordinaire, Rich Rallison, who was rumored to pour water on his lab floor where his plates were "drying".

The next morning I would sensitize them in AmDi, and shoot them after lunch. When they worked, I got almost no zero order in transmission HOE's. Which is not to say I didn't shoot objects with this process, as I did, using my trusty waffle iron as my standard test object SBR style. This process was amazingly narrow band, so much so that when I would replace the hologram on the object I could generate real time interference fringes!

Alas and alack, I have to report that this is the only way I know to make DCG; I was never successful with Jeff Blyth's veil coating technique. As always, you should try different techniques (and probably more than once!) to see what is the best system for you.

posts.author: Seventh Son
posts.content_md:
Hi JohnFP,

There is so much confusion added to all of my posts that I never know how to reply to them. Am I too vague?

I've read through a lot of posts on this site, a common thread that I see is how individuals seem to underestimate the beginning of their process (film formulation, proper gel, lab environment etc). When I see people post **Super** complicated processing techniques, my first thought is always that they need to take care of their front end problems, and not worry so much about adding a pinch of alcohol to this or a dash of Alum to that. If you get the front end right, you will be amazed at how little you will need to mess with that other stuff (of course it matters, I’m trying to make a point!).

If you want to make holograms with predictable results you need to grab hold of the variables. If you are purposefully humidifying your lab or not, your gelatin **IS** going to slurp up ambient RH. This is a **MASSIVE**variable in DCG holography! My point being, formulate your film to retard this from happening! Make your film *NEED* supplemental humidity (pre-swell). The big exception to this advice is if you make your film, and plan on immediately banging off some shots then maybe you don’t want to worry about it? But it’s a huge gamble. Is your lab more humid today than it was the last time you shot? Is it drier? These things will change the desired outcome of your shots.

I hope these comments help. 

**Danny Bee** I make HOE’s, and Display images. On this forum I am referring to display holography unless otherwise noted.

**JohnFp**, I don’t have any good advice on adding AmDi after the plate is gel coated. I’ve never gotten great results that way.

Richard Ralison dumps buckets of water on the floor, but a $25.00 humidifier from Walmart wont piss your wife off as much.

as iv stated before the holographer i learned DCG,from spray coated his plates and dipped them(later after drying),in an AMDI solution .

the RH probably doesn’t matter much before sensitizing as it become totally saturated during sensitizing stage, its important to allow the gelatin to harden so it wont dissolves during the dip (2min) in sensitizing solution.
